newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Taiwan's CPC set to boost diesel exports in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's CPC set to boost diesel exports in 1997.

text.p: Taiwan is set to boost diesel exports in 1997 as its refineries run close to full capacity, but fuel oil sales are not expected to rise due to higher domestic demand, industry sources said on Thursday.
"We have increased production resulting in excess output for exports after supplying the local market," a source with state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) told Reuters.
"Exports of diesel will become a norm for CPC and we would sell at least one to two cargoes on a regular basis each month."

The source said Taiwan's oil products demand had stabilised at an annual growth rate of three to five percent, compared with double digit growth in the early 1990s, allowing CPC to raise diesel exports.
Sources said CPC had excess diesel supplies following a rise in refining capacity late last year at its Kaohsiung and Taoyuan refineries to 770,000 barrels per day (bpd) from 600,000 bpd.
The increase was mainly due to upgrades at the 570,000-bpd Kaohsiung refinery which until recently was not able to run at full capacity due to startup teething problems.
The higher runs were aimed at meeting rising domestic fuel oil demand, industry sources said.
The CPC source said that following the addition of new crude processing units, the Kaohsiung refinery had originally planned to close its oldest crude unit which has a 50,000-bpd capacity.
But the plan had been shelved temporarily in the face of soaring product prices and it was unclear when it would be shut down, the source said.

CPC has doubled its spot exports over the past few months from the previous one 225,000-to-250,000-barrel cargo of 0.3-percent sulphur diesel a month. Since July it has also started exporting on a term basis.

In its most recent spot tender, CPC sold three cargoes for December 11-30 lifting because of higher refinery runs of up to 90 percent from its usual 80 percent. "We raised output ...(because) refining profit margin is good," said another CPC source.
The improved margins were due to a five-year peak in diesel prices which are now discussed at well above $32.00 a barrel on a free-on-board Singapore basis.
CPC's six-month term contract was first issued for cargoes lifting between July-December 1996 and this was awarded to two traders. CPC has so far sold 10 diesel cargoes through these term deals.

It has since issued a new tender to sell four to six cargoes for deliveries between January and June 1997. This tender closes on December 10 and CPC might again award two contracts if the bids were attractive, a CPC source said.
Unlike diesel, CPC's fuel oil exports are not expected to rise dramatically as Taiwan requires large volumes of low sulphur fuel oil for its power stations.

It sells 30,000 tonnes of 3.0-percent fuel oil a month and has a term contract to sell 10 cargoes in 1996 which also expires in December. It recently tendered to sell four to six cargoes for January-June 1997 deliveries, closing on December 9.

The source said the export volume would be limited as more high sulphur fuel oil would be refined into 1.0-and-0.5-percent grades so that CPC does not need to import too much low sulphur fuel oil. CPC normally imports one or two 80,000-tonne cargoes of low sulphur fuel oil every one to two months.
